strengths: Well-motivated paradigm: using face-only counterfactual edits on real photographs strikes a novel middle ground between fully synthetic/heavily-generated benchmarks (which risk generator artifacts and distribution shift) and uncontrolled real-photo benchmarks (which confound demographic effects with correlated scene factors). The FOCUS/VisBias comparison (Table 2) provides concrete evidence that this reduces confounding relative to prior uncontrolled real-image benchmarks.

REFLECT evaluation suite is thoughtfully designed with three complementary, decision-oriented task formats (2AFC, MCQ, numeric salary recommendation) that probe different output modalities (comparative, categorical, continuous), and the paper convincingly shows that bias direction/magnitude is highly sensitive to task formulation, which is a useful methodological insight for the auditing community.

Reasonably rigorous quality-control pipeline for the counterfactual dataset: localization of edits verified via face-region vs non-face-region difference metrics, and demographic label fidelity validated via an independent attribute recognizer (high accuracy reported).

Broad empirical coverage: five contemporary SOTA VLMs (GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Qwen3-VL-Plus, DeepSeek-VL2, Llama-3.2-90B-Vision) evaluated consistently across all three tasks, with appropriate statistical treatment (position-bias mitigation in 2AFC, JSD for distributional shifts, cluster-robust significance tests for salary regression) rather than relying solely on point estimates.

Transparent and detailed reporting of prompts, editing instructions, and limitations (including candid acknowledgment that face-only edits are not perfectly localized and that dataset scale/coverage is limited), which aids interpretability and reproducibility of the specific claims being made.
weaknesses: Dataset scale is small (480 images; only 8 source photos per occupation across 6 occupations), which the authors acknowledge limits generalizability; observed “disparities” could partly reflect idiosyncrasies of the small photo set rather than robust demographic effects, especially since the significance tests in Table 3 show many occupation-level and even pooled effects are not statistically significant (e.g., most GPT-5 and Gemini pooled race/gender effects have p>0.05), which somewhat undercuts the strength of the headline claim that “disparities persist under strict counterfactual control.”

The counterfactual generation process itself relies on a proprietary generative editor (Nano Banana Pro) whose own stereotype associations or subtle correlated changes (expression, hairstyle, skin exposure, age perception) could introduce confounds that are attributed to the evaluated VLMs; the QC checks (face-vs-nonface pixel difference, label consistency) verify localization and label accuracy but do not fully rule out systematic, demographically-correlated qualitative differences in how the editor renders different groups (e.g., subtle attractiveness/professionalism shifts), which could itself drive downstream VLM judgments independent of the VLM's own bias.

Demographic categorization is coarse (5 broad race categories, binary gender), limiting insight into intersectional or finer-grained bias patterns beyond the race×gender headline groupings; other salient axes (age, disability, religion-signaling attire) are not considered.

The paper is largely descriptive/benchmarking in nature: it documents that biases exist and vary by task/model but offers limited causal or mechanistic analysis of why disparities arise or diverge across tasks, and many qualitative findings (e.g., gender/race disparities in hiring-like judgments) are consistent with prior literature rather than novel insights.

No human baseline or external validity check connecting the stylized decision tasks (e.g., 2AFC “who looks more approachable” or salary guesses from a single portrait) to real-world deployment scenarios, making it unclear how strongly these findings generalize to actual high-stakes VLM use cases.

Reproducibility is partially constrained by dependence on a closed, evolving proprietary image-editing model (Nano Banana Pro) for dataset construction, and it is unclear from the manuscript whether the FOCUS dataset, code, or full experimental logs will be publicly released, which affects independent verification of both the dataset and results.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: attribution under visual confounding is a genuine gap in existing VLM bias benchmarks, and the face-only counterfactual editing paradigm is a sensible, novel way to isolate demographic effects while preserving real-image realism.

The REFLECT suite spans three complementary task formats (2AFC, MCQ, numeric salary recommendation), and the paper convincingly shows that bias magnitude/direction depends heavily on task formulation and scenario — a useful methodological finding for the bias-auditing literature beyond the specific dataset.

Reasonably rigorous quality-control pipeline: MediaPipe-based verification that edits are localized to the face region, and an attribute-recognition consistency check (high race/gender accuracy), lending some credibility to the 'face-only' claim.

Comparison against VisBias (Table 2) directly supports the central claim that uncontrolled real-image benchmarks show larger group-wise JSD than the proposed controlled counterfactual design, which is a nice validation of the core methodological premise.

Comprehensive experiments across five SOTA VLMs (GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Qwen3-VL-Plus, DeepSeek-VL2, Llama-3.2-90B) with detailed race/gender/intersectional breakdowns, and inclusion of cluster-robust significance tests in the appendix alongside effect sizes.
Full prompts, editing protocol, and dataset construction details are provided in appendices, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Small dataset scale: only 8 source photos per occupation across 6 occupations (480 images total) sharply limits statistical power and generalizability; the paper acknowledges this but it remains a substantive limitation for claims about persistent bias patterns.

Validation of demographic labels relies on GPT-4o attribute recognition — using another VLM (with its own potential biases about racial/gender visual categorization) as a 'ground truth' check is somewhat circular and not independently verified by human raters.

No human evaluation of the generated counterfactual images (realism, naturalness, absence of stereotype exaggeration despite prompt constraints); reliance is entirely on automated pipeline checks (face-localization ratio, GPT-4o attribute match), which may miss subtler artifacts (e.g., unnatural skin tones, uncanny features).

The counterfactual editing itself is not perfectly confined to the face (nonzero non-face pixel differences reported, mean ratio ~11.77 but with wide variance implied), and unintended shifts in perceived age/expression are noted as a limitation, potentially confounding the demographic attribution the paper claims to isolate.

Some key statistical results undercut the 'disparities persist' framing: several pooled significance tests in Table 3 (e.g., GPT-5 pooled race p=0.055, gender p=0.349; Gemini pooled race p=0.470) are not significant, and the paper's choice to emphasize effect sizes over significance, while justified, somewhat softens the strength of the core empirical claim.

Race is treated as five coarse, discrete, mutually exclusive visual categories imposed via image editing — this essentializes race as a purely visual/facial construct, which is scientifically and ethically fraught, and the paper does not include a discussion of these ethical considerations (e.g., consent/provenance of source photos, implications of algorithmically 'race-swapping' real people's faces).

Occupation coverage is narrow (six roles, all somewhat stereotyped by gender/prestige), and biographies for CEO/cook were generated via few-shot GPT-4o prompting rather than sourced from real-world data, which could introduce its own artifacts despite normalization steps.

MCQ and salary tasks use single deterministic queries per image without repeated sampling, so no estimate of within-model output variance/noise is provided, which would strengthen claims about the robustness of observed disparities.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely useful methodological innovation: face-only counterfactual editing of real photographs (FOCUS), which isolates demographic facial cues from correlated scene-level confounds (background, clothing, pose) that plague prior real-image VLM bias benchmarks such as VisBias.

Very thorough validation/quality-control effort that is uncommon in bias-benchmark papers: MediaPipe-based face-localization audits, demographic label-consistency checks via an independent VLM, expression-drift audits, biography leakage/quality audits, face-body gender-mismatch robustness checks, cropping/mirroring/spatial robustness, prompt-framing ablations, position-bias diagnostics, and stochastic-decoding robustness checks.

REFLECT benchmark spans three complementary decision-oriented task formats (2AFC, MCQ, numeric salary recommendation), enabling comparison of bias signals across comparative, categorical, and continuous output types rather than a single elicitation format.

Reasonably comprehensive experimental evaluation across five current-generation VLMs (GPT, Gemini, Qwen, DeepSeek, Llama) with appropriate statistical machinery (win-rate matrices, polarization indices, JSD, bootstrap confidence intervals, cluster-robust significance tests).

Additional robustness studies (cross-editor comparison with a second image editor, leave-one-template-out analysis, template-cluster bootstrap, extension to held-out occupations, an exploratory androgynous-presentation pilot) substantially strengthen confidence that the reported disparities are not artifacts of a single editing pipeline or a handful of templates.

Findings are reported with appropriate nuance (task-, model-, and occupation-dependent effects) rather than a single overclaimed 'bias direction,' and the Limitations section is candid about scope restrictions.
weaknesses: Dataset scale is modest (480 images from only 8 source photos across 6 occupations), which limits statistical power and the ability to generalize claims to broader real-world occupational/demographic diversity; this is acknowledged but not fully mitigated even with the additional two-occupation extension.

The core dataset and most main-text experiments rely on a single image-editing pipeline (Nano Banana Pro); the cross-editor robustness check is restricted to the MCQ task on a small subset (12 templates, 240 images) and does not cover 2AFC or Salary Recommendation, leaving open whether editor-specific artifacts affect the other two tasks.

Despite extensive QC, face-only edits still show non-trivial residual artifacts (e.g., 12.1% expression drift rate, permitted hairstyle/accessory changes), and while the paper argues these do not drive the main conclusions, some construct-validity uncertainty remains about whether 'face-only' truly isolates race/gender cues versus subtly altering perceived age, attractiveness, or other correlated traits.

The significance analysis for the Salary Recommendation task (Table 13) shows many occupation-level and even pooled effects that are not statistically significant (p>0.05) for several models/occupations, yet the main-text 'Key Findings' bullets emphasize effect magnitude and moderation patterns in a way that could be read as stronger than what the significance tests support; the relationship between effect-size framing and significance should be made more explicit in the main text.

Demographic scope is coarse and Western/US-centric (5 race categories drawn from BLS categories, primarily binary gender with only a small exploratory androgynous pilot at the very end), limiting the intersectional and cross-cultural generality of the claimed contribution.

The paper does not establish any external ground truth (e.g., actual salary/education base rates) against which 'disparity' can be interpreted as unwarranted bias versus reflecting real-world calibration signals correlated with appearance; this is a common limitation in this literature but is not discussed.

Overall novelty is primarily methodological/incremental (a cleaner counterfactual construction technique plus a benchmark) rather than yielding fundamentally new insights about VLM bias mechanisms; the paper's main value lies in rigor and control rather than novel scientific findings.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and important gap in VLM bias evaluation: real-photo benchmarks conflate demographic cues with correlated scene factors (background, clothing, context), while fully synthetic benchmarks lose real-image realism. The face-only counterfactual paradigm is a sensible middle ground.

Very thorough quality-control and robustness program for a benchmark paper: MediaPipe-based verification that edits are localized to the face (median 8x concentration), demographic label consistency checks (97.9% joint accuracy), face-body gender mismatch analysis, expression-drift audit, spatial/cropping/mirroring robustness, cross-editor robustness with an independent image editor, leave-one-template-out and template-cluster bootstrap analyses, decoding-stochasticity checks, and a biography leakage/quality audit. This level of validation substantially strengthens confidence in the dataset's control assumptions.

REFLECT spans three complementary, decision-oriented task formats (2AFC, MCQ, salary recommendation), and the paper convincingly shows that conclusions about bias magnitude/direction are format- and model-dependent — a useful and non-trivial empirical finding for the community.

Comparison against VisBias (an uncontrolled real-image benchmark) via JSD is a nice way to demonstrate that scene confounding can amplify or reshape measured disparities relative to the controlled FOCUS setting.

Extensive appendix experiments (occupation extension, prompt-framing ablation, androgynous-presentation pilot, significance testing with cluster-robust errors) go beyond what is typical, and the authors are transparent about limitations (residual editing artifacts, limited dataset scale, binary gender presentation).
weaknesses: The counterfactual images are generated by a proprietary black-box image editor (Nano Banana Pro / gpt-5-image) explicitly instructed to make a person 'look like' a target race/gender; this generation process could itself encode stereotypical associations (e.g., hairstyle/accessory changes, subtle body/context shifts) that are then attributed to the evaluated VLM rather than being a clean causal manipulation. The cross-editor robustness check only covers the MCQ task on a small 240-image subset, leaving 2AFC and salary recommendation without similar independent-editor validation.

Dataset scale is modest (6 occupations, 8 source photos each, 480 images), which limits generalizability of claims to 'population-level' bias despite the paper's explicit disclaimer; some appendix results (e.g., cluster-robust p-values in Table 13) show many non-significant occupation-level effects, which sits somewhat in tension with the stronger descriptive language in the main text (e.g., 'disparities persist,' 'significantly alter').

Significance testing is largely relegated to the appendix and secondary to descriptive percentage-gap and win-rate summaries in the main text; the paper's central claims rest more on effect-size visualization than on rigorously quantified statistical significance, which is only partially reconciled with the more cautious appendix results.

Facial expression drift (12.1% of edited variants) and other within-face incidental changes (perceived age, minor hairstyle/accessory shifts) are acknowledged but not fully eliminated, slightly undercutting the 'clean attribution' claim that is central to the paper's motivation.

The benchmark evaluates a fairly narrow demographic taxonomy (five race categories, primarily binary gender, androgynous presentation only as an exploratory pilot), which constrains the intersectional and identity coverage of the conclusions.
As an evaluation-only contribution, the paper does not propose or test any mitigation strategy, somewhat limiting its practical downstream impact beyond auditing.
